resources.title: External Validation of a Widely Implemented Proprietary Sepsis Prediction Model in Hospitalized Patients
resources.abstract: Importance: The Epic Sepsis Model (ESM), a proprietary sepsis prediction model, is implemented at hundreds of US hospitals. The ESM's ability to identify patients with sepsis has not been adequately evaluated despite widespread use. Objective: To externally validate the ESM in the prediction of sepsis and evaluate its potential clinical value compared with usual care. Design, Setting, and Participants: This retrospective cohort study was conducted among 27 697 patients aged 18 years or older admitted to Michigan Medicine, the academic health system of the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, with 38 455 hospitalizations between December 6, 2018, and October 20, 2019. Exposure: The ESM score, calculated every 15 minutes. Main Outcomes and Measures: Sepsis, as defined by a composite of (1) the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention surveillance criteria and (2) International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision diagnostic codes accompanied by 2 systemic inflammatory response syndrome criteria and 1 organ dysfunction criterion within 6 hours of one another. Model discrimination was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve at the hospitalization level and with prediction horizons of 4, 8, 12, and 24 hours. Model calibration was evaluated with calibration plots. The potential clinical benefit associated with the ESM was assessed by evaluating the added benefit of the ESM score compared with contemporary clinical practice (based on timely administration of antibiotics). Alert fatigue was evaluated by comparing the clinical value of different alerting strategies. Results: We identified 27 697 patients who had 38 455 hospitalizations (21 904 women [57%]; median age, 56 years [interquartile range, 35-69 years]) meeting inclusion criteria, of whom sepsis occurred in 2552 (7%). The ESM had a hospitalization-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.63 (95% CI, 0.62-0.64). The ESM identified 183 of 2552 patients with sepsis (7%) who did not receive timely administration of antibiotics, highlighting the low sensitivity of the ESM in comparison with contemporary clinical practice. The ESM also did not identify 1709 patients with sepsis (67%) despite generating alerts for an ESM score of 6 or higher for 6971 of all 38 455 hospitalized patients (18%), thus creating a large burden of alert fatigue. Conclusions and Relevance: This external validation cohort study suggests that the ESM has poor discrimination and calibration in predicting the onset of sepsis. The widespread adoption of the ESM despite its poor performance raises fundamental concerns about sepsis management on a national level.

techniques.name: Linear Bound Propagation Verification
techniques.description: Linear bound propagation verification proves that a trained neural network meets a stated property for every input in a defined region, for example that no small change to the pixels of an image alters its class, or that a controller's output stays within limits across a box of sensor readings. CROWN, the named method, replaces each neuron's activation function with two straight lines that bound it from above and below over the values that neuron can take, then works backwards from the outputs through the layers to express an upper and a lower bound on each output as a linear function of the input, and evaluates those functions over the region to obtain guaranteed numerical bounds. If the bounds show the property holds (for a classifier, that the correct class's score stays above every other class's), it is proved for the whole region; because the straight lines over-approximate the network, bounds that fail to show it leave the case undecided, so bound propagation on its own is sound but incomplete. The alpha-beta-CROWN tool tightens the bounds by tuning the lines with gradient-based optimisation and by branch and bound: for a ReLU network it splits undecided neurons into their active and inactive cases and bounds each part separately, which given enough time settles every case, making the tool complete for ReLU networks, but at a cost that can grow exponentially with the number of neurons split, so in practice each run ends as verified, falsified (a counterexample input found) or timed out. Running on graphics processors, it reaches convolutional networks with millions of parameters, larger than exact constraint solvers usually handle, at the price of leaving hard cases undecided.

example_use_cases.description: An avionics supplier's verification team checks the network that flags wildfires in airborne infrared images. For each background crop in a held-out set taken from real flight logs, it uses alpha-beta-CROWN to prove that the detector's confidence never falls as a planted fire signal grows stronger within the specified range, lists the crops where a counterexample is found, and enters the proved cases in the safety case as evidence for that consistency requirement.

A transmission system operator replaces slow time-domain simulation with a neural network that predicts whether the grid stays stable after a fault, inside the optimiser that plans generator dispatch. At each candidate dispatch its engineers use alpha-beta-CROWN to certify that the stability prediction holds for every combination of wind, solar and load within the forecast uncertainty, and raise the stability margin wherever certification fails before the plan is issued.

A pharmaceutical packaging line uses a convolutional classifier to accept or reject blister packs from camera images. Before each model release the quality team reports certified accuracy on held-out images: the share for which CROWN bounds prove that no change of up to 2/255 in any pixel can flip the decision, a bound set above the largest per-pixel noise measured on the line's cameras. A release whose certified accuracy falls well below its ordinary accuracy goes back for retraining.

limitations.description: Bound propagation on its own is incomplete: when the bounds are too loose to show the property, the case stays undecided, which is not evidence either way. Branch and bound settles more cases, but the problem is NP-complete in general, so hard cases end in a time-out. In an industrial study of an airborne wildfire detector, every query for a monotonicity property was settled, while 62 per cent of the queries for a sensor-blur property timed out.

The property must be written as a region of inputs, such as every image within a small per-pixel change of a test image or a box of sensor values, plus a linear condition on the outputs. Rotation, lighting, weather or blur are not regions of that kind; covering them means modelling them first, for example with a separate network that generates plausible blur, and the accuracy of that model then has to be argued separately.

Robustness is proved one region at a time, usually around each test input, so certified accuracy on a test set is evidence about those inputs and that perturbation only. It does not carry over to new inputs from operation, and a classifier certified around every test image can still misclassify an unperturbed image it has not seen.

It needs the whole network in a supported form (PyTorch or ONNX) and, beyond small networks, a graphics processor with enough memory: most of the tool's example configurations were tested on a 24 GB GPU, and its documented branch-and-bound support for ReLU image models reaches residual networks of about 20 layers. Layers the library does not support need their bounds written by hand, and its documented reach of millions of parameters is far below the size of large language models.

The guarantee covers the network alone. Pre-processing, sensor faults and, for a controller, the plant it drives and how errors build up over time are outside it, so a proof that a policy network never outputs an unsafe command for any state in a box does not show that the controlled system stays safe; that needs a separate analysis of the closed loop.

resources.title: Efficient Neural Network Robustness Certification with General Activation Functions
resources.abstract: Finding minimum distortion of adversarial examples and thus certifying robustness in neural networks classifiers is known to be a challenging problem. Nevertheless, recently it has been shown to be possible to give a non-trivial certified lower bound of minimum distortion, and some recent progress has been made towards this direction by exploiting the piece-wise linear nature of ReLU activations. However, a generic robustness certification for \textit{general} activation functions still remains largely unexplored. To address this issue, in this paper we introduce CROWN, a general framework to certify robustness of neural networks with general activation functions. The novelty in our algorithm consists of bounding a given activation function with linear and quadratic functions, hence allowing it to tackle general activation functions including but not limited to the four popular choices: ReLU, tanh, sigmoid and arctan. In addition, we facilitate the search for a tighter certified lower bound by \textit{adaptively} selecting appropriate surrogates for each neuron activation. Experimental results show that CROWN on ReLU networks can notably improve the certified lower bounds compared to the current state-of-the-art algorithm Fast-Lin, while having comparable computational efficiency. Furthermore, CROWN also demonstrates its effectiveness and flexibility on networks with general activation functions, including tanh, sigmoid and arctan.

techniques.name: Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law Risk and Impact Assessment
techniques.description: HUDERIA is the Council of Europe's methodology for identifying and assessing the risks an AI system poses to human rights, democracy and the rule of law, and for planning how to prevent or reduce them, from design through deployment to retirement. It is non-binding guidance that public and private organisations may use or adapt in whole or in part; it was drawn up to support risk assessment in line with the Council of Europe's Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, and the human rights treaties its resources cite are illustrative, binding only the states that are parties to them. A multidisciplinary team first runs a context-based risk analysis (COBRA): it scopes the system's purpose, data and affected groups, works through risk factors in the system's application, design and deployment contexts, maps potential impacts on specific rights and on democratic and legal processes, gives each impact an initial rating, and triages the system, deciding whether further assessment is needed and whether the system should be built or deployed at all. Impacts are rated for severity, judged by scale (how serious the harm is), scope (how many people, which groups and for how long) and reversibility (whether those affected can be restored to their earlier position), and for probability; for systems that may pose significant risks, the team may engage affected stakeholders and then re-examines and re-rates each impact in a fuller risk and impact assessment. The output is a mitigation plan that prefers avoiding a harm to reducing, repairing or compensating for it, names who is responsible for each measure, outlines where appropriate the remedies open to affected people, and schedules repeat reviews as the system and its context change.

example_use_cases.description: A city council's children's services department is offered a model that ranks safeguarding referrals for follow-up. A team of caseworkers, a data scientist and a human rights lawyer runs the context-based risk analysis, maps impacts on family life, non-discrimination and fair procedure, and at triage asks whether existing caseworker screening would serve the problem better and whether the referral data represent the families concerned, before deciding whether to procure the model at all.

A recruitment software company assessing a CV-screening model engages disabled and older job seekers, the groups its analysis found most exposed, then rates each mapped impact for scale, scope, reversibility and probability under a scoring rule it writes down. Its mitigation plan drops a feature that scored video interviews, an 'avoid' measure, rather than relying on correcting decisions afterwards, and names the owner of each remaining measure.

A national tax authority that assessed its fraud-risk model before launch repeats the risk and impact assessment when it adds bank-transaction data, and again when a change in benefit rules alters who is flagged. Each review updates the mitigation plan and the information and appeal routes offered to people wrongly flagged, so the assessment on file describes the system as it now runs.

A health ministry outside Europe adapts HUDERIA for a symptom-checker chatbot, keeping the treaty references in the risk-factor and impact lists only for the instruments its state is party to and adding its own constitution, health law and data protection law, while keeping the four elements and the severity variables so that its assessments follow a published structure others can recognise and check.

limitations.description: HUDERIA leaves the rule for combining scale, scope, reversibility and probability into a risk level, and the thresholds used at triage, to the authorities or project teams applying it. Two teams can rate the same system differently and both be following the methodology, so an assessment can be compared or checked only if the team records the scoring rule it chose and why.

Stakeholder engagement and the detailed risk and impact assessment are optional, and are expected mainly for systems that the team's own triage finds may pose significant risks. A team that under-rates a system at triage can skip the stages most likely to expose the problem, so the evidence is stronger when someone outside the team has reviewed the triage reasoning.

The assessment rests on documents, expert judgement and what stakeholders report; it does not test the system. Probability ratings made before a system is built can be little more than informed estimates, so claims about how the system actually behaves, for example whether it treats groups differently, need test results from other techniques alongside the assessment.

HUDERIA assesses one system at a time. It asks teams to consider cumulative effects when a system runs alongside others serving similar purposes, which is where many harms to democratic and legal processes arise, but gives no method for estimating them. An assessment can therefore find each system acceptable while their combined contribution to a wider harm goes unmeasured, so claims about societal impact need evidence beyond a single assessment.

A full assessment needs people who can judge impacts on rights in law as well as people who understand the system's data and design, and it is meant to be repeated over the system's life. Organisations without access to human rights legal expertise may be unable to carry out the impact mapping and mitigation planning to the depth the methodology intends.

techniques.name: AI Incident Reporting with the OECD Common Reporting Framework
techniques.description: AI incident reporting with the OECD common reporting framework records each event in which an AI system caused harm, or could plausibly have caused it, in the common set of 29 fields the OECD published in February 2025, so that reports from different organisations, sectors and countries can be compared and pooled. The framework is meant for both mandatory and voluntary reporting and defines what a report contains, not the reporting interface or what should happen afterwards. The reporter first classifies the event using the OECD's definitions: an AI incident is an event in which the development, use or malfunction of an AI system directly or indirectly leads to harm to people's health, disruption of critical infrastructure, a violation of human rights or of laws protecting fundamental, labour or intellectual property rights, or harm to property, communities or the environment, and an AI hazard is one that could plausibly lead to such harm. Seven fields are mandatory: a title, a description, how the AI system was involved (as a direct cause, a contributing factor, a failure to act, through over-reliance or misuse, through human error, or through a failure to comply with the law), who is reporting, supporting material, the severity (hazard, serious hazard, incident, serious incident or disaster) and the type of harm. The other 22 record, where known and among other things, when and where it happened, the system and the organisations behind it, the people affected, the sector, how widely the system was deployed, whether training data, the model or several interacting systems were involved, the system's task and level of autonomy, and any action taken, giving an inspectable register of what went wrong in operation.

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank's model risk team logs every complaint from customers or staff about its credit, fraud and customer-chatbot models that meets the OECD definition of an AI incident or hazard. A wrongly refused loan, an account frozen by a fraud alert and a chatbot quoting the wrong fees are recorded on the same severity scale and harm types, with the model and version and how the model was involved, so the quarterly risk committee can see which systems recur and which harms dominate.

A hospital records near misses as well as harms. When a radiologist notices that the imaging triage model has put an urgent scan at the back of the queue, the event is logged as an AI hazard, with the model's erroneous ranking as a direct cause, its autonomy recorded as human-in-the-loop, and the action taken, so that patterns of near misses are visible before one becomes an incident.

A national regulator that receives AI incident reports from deployers in several sectors asks for them in the OECD format, with a published note on how it judges seriousness, so that it can count serious incidents by sector and harm type and compare its figures with those of other authorities using the same fields.

A city transport authority running an AI traffic-signal optimiser records a period of emergency-vehicle delays as an incident affecting critical infrastructure, with the system as a contributing factor and an operator's configuration change as human error, so the record shows both causes and the follow-up actions assigned to the supplier and to its own staff.

limitations.description: A register is only as complete as the reports that reach it. Harms nobody notices, such as people quietly refused a service, and events staff have reasons not to report go unrecorded, so a short register is weak evidence that a system has caused little harm unless the organisation can also show how incidents are detected and how reporting is encouraged.

The OECD's own definitions say that seriousness is highly context-dependent, that each jurisdiction may define it differently, and that several small incidents can add up to a serious one. Two reporters can classify the same event differently, so counts of serious incidents can be compared only between reporters that share a written severity rule.

The framework standardises what is recorded, not how an incident is investigated or fixed, and the OECD paper explicitly gives no guidance on corrective or preventive action. Its field for how the AI system was involved is a short category list, and the fields on training data and the model are optional free text, so an organisation needs its own root-cause and follow-up process if records are to lead to changes.

None of the seven mandatory fields identifies the system or its version, the organisation that deployed it or the date of the event. Records kept to the mandatory minimum cannot trace incidents to a model release or show repeated failures of one system; the framework lets a reporting scheme make more fields mandatory, and an organisation that needs this traceability has to do so.

The framework is a recent proposal that the OECD planned to test through open submissions to its AI Incidents Monitor. Regulators that impose a legal duty to report incidents set their own format, categories and deadlines, so an organisation under such a duty reports in the regulator's format, may need to keep the OECD fields alongside, and cannot assume that an event serious on the OECD scale meets the legal definition of a serious incident, or the reverse.

techniques.name: SMACTR Internal Algorithmic Audit
techniques.description: SMACTR is an internal audit procedure for AI systems, proposed by Raji and colleagues in 2020, in which an audit team inside the developing organisation but separate from the product team examines a system during development and before launch against the ethical objectives and requirements the organisation has declared for it. The audit runs in five stages, each producing set documents. In Scoping, auditors review the product requirements and the declared objectives and write an ethical review of the use case, drawing in independent domain experts and marginalised groups, and a social impact assessment; in Mapping, they map the people involved, review existing design records, interview the engineers and begin a failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA), a systematic review of the foreseeable ways the system could fail and their effects, used to rank risks for testing. In Artefact Collection, a checklist confirms that the expected development documents, such as model cards and datasheets, exist; in Testing, auditors run tests chosen from the FMEA's priorities, such as adversarial probing with tailored inputs, and rate each risk high, mid or low from its likelihood and severity in an ethical risk analysis chart; in Reflection, they set the results against the declared objectives, finalise the risk analysis and agree a remediation plan with the engineering team. The documents are kept in an algorithmic design history file, from which the auditors write a summary report that leadership can use to decide whether the system launches, changes or is abandoned.

example_use_cases.description: An insurer's internal audit team audits a claims-triage model before launch. Interviews in Mapping reveal that a field used as a proxy for chronic illness was dropped late without the requirements being updated; the FMEA ranks under-prioritising complex claims as the top risk, so Testing concentrates on claims from people with several conditions, and the summary report goes to the risk committee with a remediation plan and a recommendation to delay launch.

A software company's responsible-AI audit team audits a customer-support chatbot. Artefact Collection finds no datasheet for the fine-tuning conversations, so the auditors require the product team to write one before testing; prompts drawn from the FMEA then test whether the bot discloses other customers' account details or gives poorer answers to customers writing in non-standard English, and the ethical risk chart and remediation plan record what must change before release.

A government digital service's audit team, which reports to the agency's chief risk officer rather than to the delivery programme, audits an in-house model that prioritises housing repair requests before it replaces manual triage. The chief risk officer uses the summary report to decide whether the model goes live, and the design history file and report are filed where the agency's external auditors and ombudsman can later inspect them.

limitations.description: The auditors are employees of the organisation they audit and share its interests; the authors acknowledge that independence is hard to keep and that audits risk becoming reputation management. Findings carry more weight when the audit team reports outside the product's management line and the design history file can be examined by an outside party.

The system is judged against the ethical objectives the organisation declares for it, which the authors note have been criticised as vague, and the paper leaves open what level of performance, for example how close to parity across groups, counts as acceptable. A clean audit shows consistency with the standards and thresholds the organisation chose to declare, and says nothing about any external standard it did not adopt.

The Testing stage prescribes no particular tests; the authors expect tests to vary widely by system and to follow the FMEA's priorities. What the audit can show about the system's behaviour therefore depends on the tests the team chooses, and a failure mode the FMEA did not foresee is likely to go untested.

The audit is deliberately slow and document-heavy, and the authors note that fast, iterative development is hard to audit. Its results describe the system at the time of the audit, so a model retrained or reconfigured afterwards is not covered unless the relevant stages are repeated.

The paper does not say which systems should be audited or in how much depth, leaving that to the organisation, and it illustrates the procedure only on two hypothetical client projects. Published evidence of how well it finds problems in real systems is limited.

techniques.name: Data Validation Checks
techniques.description: Data validation checks apply a written set of rules about what valid data look like to every new batch of data before a model is trained on it or uses it to make predictions, and flag or hold back any batch that breaks them. In Great Expectations (GX Core), a widely used open-source library for this, each rule is an expectation, a declarative assertion such as that a column exists and has a given type, has no missing values or takes values only from an allowed set or within a range (rules on single values can allow a stated share of rows to fail), or keeps a summary statistic (its mean, a quantile, or the divergence of its histogram from one built on reference data) within bounds the team sets. Expectations are grouped into a suite that a checkpoint runs on each batch as it arrives; the result records for every rule whether it passed and how many values broke it, with examples, configured actions can alert the team or update a human-readable report, and the pipeline can be set to stop training or scoring on a batch that failed. Running the same suite on training batches and on the data a deployed model receives catches differences between the two, such as a feature that is always missing in production, before they degrade predictions; unlike out-of-distribution detectors, the checks need no model and judge whole batches against explicit rules rather than scoring single inputs, and unlike runtime monitoring of a deployed model they act before the model sees the data. Unlike a kernel two-sample test, its distribution rules are fixed bounds set by the team, not a statistical test of whether two samples differ.

example_use_cases.description: An air navigation service provider feeds surveillance track reports into a model that predicts aircraft arrival times. Its data engineers run an expectation suite on every incoming batch, covering required fields, units, plausible ranges for altitude and ground speed, and the share of reports with missing positions, so that a sensor change that silently switched altitude from feet to metres would stop the batch before it reached the model rather than surface weeks later as worse predictions.

A weather service that retrains a statistical correction model each month on station observations validates every monthly extract first: station identifiers must come from the station list, temperatures must lie within each station's climatological limits, no variable may have more than 2 per cent missing values, and each variable's mean and quantiles must stay within bounds set from earlier years. A failed check stops the retraining and opens a ticket listing the failing stations.

A hospital running a deterioration-risk model on laboratory results checks each hourly batch from the laboratory system against expectations for test codes, units and value ranges, so that if a laboratory changes the unit of a test without notice the batch is flagged and risk scores for the affected patients are withheld until the mapping is corrected.

A bank's credit-scoring team runs the expectation suite written for its training data on a daily sample of the applications its deployed model scores and compares the results, so that a field the online form has stopped collecting, which the scoring service quietly fills with a default value, shows up as a difference between training and production data rather than as an unexplained drop in approval rates.

limitations.description: Checks catch only what someone thought to write down. A batch can satisfy every rule and still be wrong in a way no rule covers, such as a changed relationship between two columns or a change in how labels were assigned. GX Core does not infer rules from the data, since its automatic profilers were removed in version 1.0, so each rule has to be specified, and for pipelines with thousands of features that effort can put teams off setting up validation at all.

Bounds for distribution rules are hard to set. Statistical tests on large batches fire on differences too small to matter: in Google's data validation paper, a chi-square test between 100 million points and a copy with 0.01 per cent of them redrawn from a wider distribution raised an alert in 7 of 10 trials, while thresholds on divergence measures such as KL divergence are hard for teams to interpret. Bounds are therefore tuned by trial, risking too many alerts or missed shifts.

The rules describe the input data, not the model's performance. A batch that passes can still produce wrong predictions if the relationship between inputs and outcomes has changed (concept drift), and a batch that fails shows that the data changed, not that predictions got worse, so the checks need pairing with monitoring of performance once outcomes arrive.

Alerts help only if someone acts on them, and rules need upkeep as data legitimately change. In Google's deployment across more than 700 pipelines, new columns, unexpected values and missing columns were the commonest anomalies, most pipelines revised their schema, and between 28 and 100 per cent of fired anomalies of each kind were fixed, which the authors attribute partly to operators missing or ignoring alerts.

The checks work on tables: GX Core connects to data frames, SQL databases and data files, so for images, audio, free text or gridded weather fields the team must first compute a table of properties, such as sizes, value ranges or missing tiles, and write rules about those. This catches broken or truncated inputs but not changes in what the content shows.

techniques.name: Metamorphic Testing
techniques.description: Metamorphic testing checks a model or AI system without needing the correct output for each test input, by checking that the outputs for related inputs stand in a relation that must hold if the system works as intended. The tester first writes metamorphic relations from knowledge of the task, each pairing a change to the input with the change it should cause in the output, or with no change: adding fog to a road image should leave a steering prediction within a set tolerance, adding a few stray sensor points outside the road area should not remove any detected obstacle, and rotating a whole flight scenario should leave its outcome unchanged. Existing test inputs (source cases) are transformed into follow-up inputs according to each relation, the system is run on both, and each pair is checked, with numeric outputs often allowed a tolerance. A violation points to a fault or unwanted behaviour without any labelled answer, unless the relation itself is wrong; the output is the violation rate for each relation with the failing pairs, and a relation that holds on every pair shows only that the outputs agree with each other, not that they are right. Prompt robustness testing and causal discrimination testing in this catalogue each apply one family of invariance relations (meaning-preserving changes to a prompt, and a change of protected attribute), and prompt robustness testing also scores the answers against known ones; metamorphic testing is the general procedure for writing and checking any such relation, including relations that say how the output should change, and needs no known answers.

example_use_cases.description: An air navigation service provider evaluating a machine-learning conflict-detection aid for en-route controllers has no ground truth for most replayed traffic samples. Its test team writes three relations: swapping two aircraft's call signs, shifting every timestamp by the same amount, and rotating the whole sample together with its wind field must not change which aircraft pairs are flagged. It runs them on a year of recorded traffic and holds the release until every violation is explained.

A supplier of lidar obstacle perception for driverless shuttles cannot label every frame it records. Following a relation implied by the perception specification, its test team adds a few hundred random points outside the mapped road area to recorded frames and checks that no obstacle detected in the original frame disappears, reporting the share of frames where one does, by number of points added, as a release criterion for each software build.

A weather service testing a neural network that nowcasts rainfall from radar images checks a relation expected from the way rain moves with the wind: away from the domain's edges, shifting the input radar sequence a few grid cells east should shift the forecast rain field by the same amount, within a tolerance set from the model's day-to-day error. Forecasters review the breaking cases to judge whether the model has learnt a dependence on location, such as on terrain, that it should keep.

A bank moving its credit-scoring models to a new library cannot treat every difference from the old library's outputs as a fault, since the solvers differ. Its validation team writes relations the mathematics guarantees: reordering the input columns, or adding a constant to a numeric input in training and scoring data of a logistic regression with an unpenalised intercept, must leave every predicted probability unchanged within solver tolerance. Each violation is investigated as a fault.

limitations.description: Passing shows that outputs are consistent, not that they are correct. A model that gives the same wrong answer for a source case and its follow-up satisfies the relation, and one that is wrong in the same way everywhere can pass every invariance relation. On its own the technique therefore does not suit systems where each output must be shown to be right, and it complements rather than replaces testing against known answers where those exist.

The evidence is only as good as the relations, which are written by hand from domain knowledge, with no systematic way to choose among the many possible ones. A relation the system is not bound to obey produces false alarms: in a study of the Weka library, violations by its nearest-neighbour classifier came from legitimate tie-breaking between equally likely labels, not from faults. An incomplete set of relations gives false confidence.

Most model outputs need a tolerance, and the result depends heavily on it. In the DeepTest study of three driving models, violations under simple image transformations fell from 23,391 when a transformed frame's squared error against the human steering label could be at most the original mean squared error to 330 when it could be five times that, and manual review still found false positives. Counts compare only between runs with the same tolerance, set from what the application can accept.

Follow-up inputs are synthetic and may not occur in practice: rain or fog added to an image, or points scattered into a lidar frame, approximate real conditions without reproducing them. A violation on an unrealistic input may not matter in operation, and a pass covers only the transformations tried, so the evidence is about the tested relations and transformations, not the operating conditions as a whole.

A model whose outputs vary between runs on the same input, through sampling, seeds or GPU arithmetic, breaks relations by chance, so runs must be made repeatable or each case repeated and judged statistically. This bites hardest for relations over the training data, such as Xie et al.'s for classifiers, which need the model retrained for every follow-up case; for models that are costly to train only prediction-time relations are practical, and they test the trained model, not its training.

resources.title: Metamorphic Testing: A New Approach for Generating Next Test Cases
resources.abstract: In software testing, a set of test cases is constructed according to some predefined selection criteria. The software is then examined against these test cases. Three interesting observations have been made on the current artifacts of software testing. Firstly, an error-revealing test case is considered useful while a successful test case which does not reveal software errors is usually not further investigated. Whether these successful test cases still contain useful information for revealing software errors has not been properly studied. Secondly, no matter how extensive the testing has been conducted in the development phase, errors may still exist in the software [5]. These errors, if left undetected, may eventually cause damage to the production system. The study of techniques for uncovering software errors in the production phase is seldom addressed in the literature. Thirdly, as indicated by Weyuker in [6], the availability of test oracles is pragmatically unattainable in most situations. However, the availability of test oracles is generally assumed in conventional software testing techniques. In this paper, we propose a novel test case selection technique that derives new test cases from the successful ones. The selection aims at revealing software errors that are possibly left undetected in successful test cases which may be generated using some existing strategies. As such, the proposed technique augments the effectiveness of existing test selection strategies. The technique also helps uncover software errors in the production phase and can be used in the absence of test oracles.

techniques.name: Reliability Diagram with Expected Calibration Error
techniques.description: A reliability diagram with expected calibration error (ECE) measures whether a classifier's stated confidence matches how often it is right, so that a reader can tell whether predictions given a probability of 70 per cent come true about 70 per cent of the time. Using labelled cases the model was not trained on, each prediction's confidence (the probability given to the predicted class, or to an event such as rain above a threshold) is placed in one of a fixed number of bins, commonly ten or fifteen equal-width intervals between 0 and 1, and in each bin the average confidence is compared with the observed frequency, the share of its cases in which the predicted class or event actually occurred. The reliability diagram plots observed frequency against average confidence bin by bin, so that bins below the diagonal show overconfidence and bins above it underconfidence, and is usually shown with a histogram of how many cases fall in each bin, which the diagram itself does not show; the ECE condenses the same comparison into one number, the average gap between confidence and observed frequency weighted by each bin's share of the cases, and the maximum calibration error reports the largest gap in any bin. The technique measures and changes nothing: Platt scaling, isotonic regression calibration and temperature scaling repair a model's probabilities, and this measurement, run before and after on the same held-out cases, none of them used to fit the repair, is the evidence that a repair worked.

example_use_cases.description: A national meteorological service is deciding whether to issue a neural-network nowcast's probabilities that radar reflectivity will exceed set thresholds within the next hour. On a held-out season of radar composites, its verification team draws reliability diagrams with sample-count histograms and computes the ECE for each threshold and lead time beside those of its current extrapolation ensemble, and issues the new probabilities only for thresholds where they are at least as reliable.

A hospital's imaging AI group receives a chest X-ray classifier whose vendor reports good calibration on public data. Before connecting it, the group computes the reliability diagram and ECE on a year of its own labelled studies, finds the model overconfident in its highest bins, fits temperature scaling on a separate validation split, and repeats the measurement on the untouched test split to show whether the gap has closed.

A law firm's knowledge team evaluating a language-model research assistant that reports a confidence with each answer asks it a held-out set of questions with verified answers, bins its self-reported confidence, and computes the reliability diagram and ECE for each practice area rather than only for the whole set. The confidence display is switched off for practice areas where the gap between stated confidence and accuracy exceeds the firm's threshold.

A card issuer's fraud team checks its transaction-risk model each month on transactions whose outcomes have arrived, using bins fixed at validation that are narrow over the high scores where alerts are raised. Because fraud is rare, nearly all cases fall in the lowest bin and dominate the ECE, so the team tracks the gap in each high-score bin as well; a gap above the limit set at model sign-off triggers an investigation of drift and a decision on recalibration.

limitations.description: The result depends on how predictions are binned. With equal-width bins, confident models put most cases in one or two bins, which dominate the ECE while the others rest on few cases; more bins give a finer measurement but a noisier estimate in each bin. Rankings of recalibration methods can change with the number of bins or the binning scheme, so both must be reported and held fixed in any comparison.

Binning distorts the estimate in both directions. Overconfident and underconfident predictions in the same bin cancel, so with plenty of data the binned ECE understates the true error. On small samples, sampling noise inflates it: with 15 equal-width bins, a simulated perfectly calibrated model showed large errors on 200 cases. ECEs from samples of different sizes, such as subgroups, are not directly comparable; equal-mass bins or a debiased estimator reduce the bias.

Calibration says nothing about how well the model separates cases. A model that gives every case the overall base rate, such as 0.5 on a balanced dataset, is calibrated but useless, so the ECE must be reported with accuracy, the area under the ROC curve or a proper scoring rule such as the Brier score, which combines calibration with how decisive the predictions are.

Weighting by bin size gives rare but important predictions almost no weight. In a precipitation nowcasting study, almost all probabilities for heavy-rain thresholds fell in the lowest bin, so the ECE barely registered the rare high-probability forecasts, and at the highest threshold it could not be compared because some bins were empty. For multi-class models the usual ECE also looks only at the top predicted class and ignores the calibration of the others.

The measurement holds only for the population and period it was computed on. One ECE over a whole test set can hide large differences between subgroups: in an evaluation of language models answering medical questions, ECE ranged from 0.041 to 0.141 across specialties, a spread the pooled figure masked. Calibration can also drift after deployment, so it has to be measured for the subgroups that matter and repeated on new labelled data.

resources.abstract: Confidence calibration -- the problem of predicting probability estimates representative of the true correctness likelihood -- is important for classification models in many applications. We discover that modern neural networks, unlike those from a decade ago, are poorly calibrated. We evaluate the performance of various post-processing calibration methods on state-of-the-art architectures with image and document classification datasets. Our analysis and experiments not only offer insights into neural network learning, but also provide a simple and straightforward recipe for practical settings: on most datasets, temperature scaling -- a single-parameter variant of Platt Scaling -- is surprisingly effective at calibrating predictions.

resources.abstract: Objective: To evaluate the alignment between self-reported confidence of large language models (LLM) and their accuracy in answering medical multiple-choice questions. Materials and Methods: We prompted six LLMs (GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5-nano, GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Gemini 2.5) to answer MedMCQA items and report confidence scores. Based on 12,000 LLM responses, we calculated Expected Calibration Errors (ECE) by averaging absolute differences between observed accuracy and predicted confidence. Results: Mean ECE differed by model (Claude Sonnet 4.5 best: 0.06; Gpt-4o worst: 0.127) and varied across specialties (“Skin” best: 0.041; “Social & Preventive Medicine” worst: 0.141). Accuracy of examined LLMs showed analogous variation between specialties. Discussion: Our results demonstrate that high accuracy does not guarantee reliable uncertainty estimation. We identified substantial heterogeneity across medical specialties, where pooled metrics masked a threefold ECE increase between best- and worst-performing domains. Conclusion: We recommend incorporating calibration reporting into LLM evaluations, as larger models exhibit improved “self-knowledge”, but uneven overconfidence persists.

techniques.name: Continuous Ranked Probability Score
techniques.description: The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) measures the quality of a probabilistic forecast of a numerical quantity, such as tomorrow's temperature or next week's demand, by scoring the whole predicted distribution, not just a single best guess, against the value later observed. For each case it compares the forecast's cumulative distribution (the predicted probability that the outcome will fall below each possible value) with a step that jumps from 0 to 1 at the observed value, squares the gap at every value and adds these up, which is the same as adding up the Brier score of the yes-or-no forecasts 'the outcome will be below this value' over every possible threshold. For a forecast given as an ensemble or a sample it can be computed as the average distance between the members and the observation minus half the average distance between pairs of members, closed forms exist for common distributions such as the Gaussian, and for a single-value forecast it reduces to the absolute error, so probabilistic and deterministic forecasts can be compared directly. The score is proper: a forecaster expects the best score by reporting the distribution they actually believe, so it cannot be improved on average by making forecasts narrower or wider than warranted, and it is lowest when the forecast distribution matches how outcomes actually vary. Scores are averaged over many cases, are in the units of the forecast quantity with lower values better, and are often reported as a skill score relative to a reference forecast such as climatology (the long-run historical distribution), giving evidence for claims about the accuracy of a forecaster's probabilities by variable, location and lead time.

example_use_cases.description: A national weather service deciding whether to run a machine-learning ensemble alongside its physics-based ensemble scores both against a year of station observations, computing the fair CRPS (the two ensembles differ in size) for 2-metre temperature and 10-metre wind at every station and lead time. It adopts the new system only for the variables and lead times where its CRPS skill relative to the existing ensemble is positive.

A wind-farm operator choosing between two vendors of probabilistic power forecasts for day-ahead trading receives 19 quantiles per hour from each. It approximates each forecast's CRPS by averaging the quantile scores across those levels and compares the vendors over a full winter against metered output. Because high-output hours drive balancing costs, it also compares them on a version of the score weighted towards the upper quantiles, averaged over all hours, not only those with high output.

A hospital group's capacity team plans elective admissions with a probabilistic forecast of bed occupancy one week ahead. Each week it computes the forecast's CRPS against the occupancy that followed and its skill score against a seasonal naive forecast, and a rolling eight-week skill score below zero triggers a review of the model before it is used for the next planning cycle.

limitations.description: One CRPS value combines calibration (whether outcomes behave like draws from the forecast distribution) and sharpness (how narrow the forecast is), so a better score does not show which improved, and an average over many cases can hide conditions in which forecasts are consistently too narrow or too wide. A claim about calibration needs Hersbach's decomposition of the score into reliability and resolution parts, a rank histogram or a spread-skill check as well.

Every threshold carries equal weight and extreme outcomes are rare, so the average score says little about how well extremes are forecast; WeatherBench 2 notes that the CRPS does not specifically focus on extreme weather. Averaging only over cases in which an extreme occurred does not repair this and can discredit skilful forecasters (Lerch et al. 2017); claims about warnings of extremes need a threshold-weighted CRPS that emphasises the tails.

It scores one quantity at one place and lead time at a time, so it does not test whether a forecast gets the relationships between places, times or variables right. WeatherBench 2 notes that its CRPS results ignore spatial and temporal correlation, and found models trained on each wind component separately biased in wind speed; claims about joint quantities, such as rainfall totalled over a catchment, need a multivariate score such as the energy score.

The score is in the units of the forecast quantity and grows with how variable that quantity is, so raw values cannot be compared or pooled across variables, locations or seasons with different variability, and averages are dominated by the most variable cases. Comparisons across these need a skill score relative to a stated reference forecast, and the choice of reference, such as climatology or persistence, changes the result.

For an ensemble, the usual estimate treats the members as the whole forecast distribution, which penalises small ensembles: if two systems draw members from the same distribution, the one with fewer members scores worse on average. Ferro (2014) showed the usual ensemble CRPS is unfair in this sense and gave an adjusted fair version, which libraries such as scoringrules provide; it should be used whenever ensembles of different sizes are compared.

techniques.name: Kernel Two-Sample Test (Maximum Mean Discrepancy)
techniques.description: A kernel two-sample test checks whether two sets of data could have come from the same distribution; in assurance it is used to check whether the inputs a deployed model now receives still resemble the data on which it was validated, and to detect when they stop doing so. Its statistic, the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), is built from a kernel, a function that scores how similar two data points are (commonly a Gaussian function of the distance between them), and in its usual squared form it is the average similarity among points in the reference sample, plus the average similarity among points in the new sample, minus twice the average similarity between points from different samples. With a characteristic kernel such as the Gaussian, the population value is zero only when the two distributions are identical, so the test can respond to any kind of difference, including a change in how features vary together that tests applied to one feature at a time cannot see, and kernels exist for strings and graphs as well as numerical vectors. To obtain a p-value, the two samples are pooled and repeatedly divided at random into groups of the original sizes, the statistic is recomputed for each division, and the p-value is the share of divisions giving a value at least as large as the one observed; high-dimensional inputs such as images are usually first reduced to a short vector, for example the code of an autoencoder or the model's predicted class probabilities. The output, for each window of new data, is the MMD value and its p-value at a stated significance level, which shows whether that window differs detectably from the reference, but not whether the difference affects the model's accuracy.

example_use_cases.description: A card issuer's model-risk team tests a random sample of each night's transactions, at most one per customer, against a fixed sample from the fraud model's validation period, after standardising the input features. It set the significance level so that, with nothing changed, it expects about one false alarm a quarter, and a significant result triggers a check of the model's accuracy on newly labelled cases before its alert thresholds are relied on the next day.

Before switching on a chest X-ray triage model at a second hospital that uses a different make of scanner, the deploying team compares 500 recent images from the new site with 500 from the validation set. Each image is first reduced to a short vector by an autoencoder trained on validation images. A significant difference sends the model for local validation on labelled cases from the new site instead of relying on its original results.

A customer-service team whose question-answering assistant was evaluated on a fixed test set compares the sentence embeddings of each week's user questions with those of the test set. When a week is flagged, it computes the MMD witness function, which scores each question by how much more it resembles the new week's questions than the test set, reads the top-scoring questions, finds queries about a new product, and adds such questions to the test set.

limitations.description: A significant result shows that inputs differ from the reference, not that the model has got worse: Rabanser et al. note that distributions shift constantly and often harmlessly, and with large windows the test can flag differences too small to matter. A drift alarm becomes evidence about performance only when followed by an accuracy check on labelled cases, and an absence of alarms reassures only if the test was shown beforehand to detect the shifts that harm the model.

On raw high-dimensional inputs the test has little power: in Rabanser et al.'s comparison on image data the multivariate test performed poorly without first reducing the dimension. The reduction then decides what can be seen, since a change that leaves the autoencoder code or predicted probabilities unchanged goes undetected. The kernel's width matters too: it is usually set to the median distance between points, which Gretton et al. call a heuristic, the best width being an open question.

The statistic compares every pair of points, so its cost grows with the square of the combined sample size, and the permutation test repeats it many times; Rabanser et al. ran kernel tests only up to 1,000 new samples for this reason. Gretton et al.'s linear-time version is far cheaper but needs much more data for the same power, so high-volume monitoring has to trade window size, detection delay and computing cost against each other.

The permutation p-value assumes that observations within each sample are independent. Consecutive sensor readings, transactions from one customer or successive time steps are correlated, and shuffling them breaks that dependence, so the test signals a difference far more often than its stated level: in Chwialkowski et al.'s experiments on autocorrelated signals the permutation test almost always rejected when nothing had changed. Such data need thinning or a wild bootstrap.

Run on every new window at the conventional 5 per cent level, the test flags about one window in twenty even when nothing has changed, which for daily windows means around 18 false alarms a year. Continuous monitoring needs a stricter level, a correction for repeated testing, or an online version of the test whose threshold is set for an expected run time between false alarms.

resources.title: A Kernel Two-Sample Test
resources.abstract: We propose a framework for analyzing and comparing distributions, which we use to construct statistical tests to determine if two samples are drawn from different distributions.  Our test statistic is the largest difference in expectations over functions in the unit ball of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), and is called the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD).  We present two distribution-free tests based on large deviation bounds for the MMD, and a third test based on the asymptotic distribution of this statistic.  The MMD can be computed in quadratic time, although efficient linear time approximations are available.  Our statistic is an instance of an integral probability metric, and various classical metrics on distributions are obtained when alternative function classes are used in place of an RKHS.  We apply our two-sample tests  to a variety of problems, including attribute matching for databases using the Hungarian marriage method, where they perform strongly.  Excellent performance is also obtained when comparing distributions over graphs, for which these are the first such tests.

Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift
resources.abstract: We might hope that when faced with unexpected inputs, well-designed software systems would fire off warnings. Machine learning (ML) systems, however, which depend strongly on properties of their inputs (e.g. the i.i.d. assumption), tend to fail silently. This paper explores the problem of building ML systems that fail loudly, investigating methods for detecting dataset shift, identifying exemplars that most typify the shift, and quantifying shift malignancy. We focus on several datasets and various perturbations to both covariates and label distributions with varying magnitudes and fractions of data affected. Interestingly, we show that across the dataset shifts that we explore, a two-sample-testing-based approach, using pre-trained classifiers for dimensionality reduction, performs best. Moreover, we demonstrate that domain-discriminating approaches tend to be helpful for characterizing shifts qualitatively and determining if they are harmful.

sample_claims.text: Applied to autoencoder representations of 500 images from each source, the kernel two-sample test found no significant difference at the 1 per cent level between the new hospital's chest X-rays and the validation images, and the same test detected the simulated scanner changes that had reduced the model's accuracy in validation.

Every alarm raised by the nightly kernel two-sample test on the fraud model's inputs in the past six months was followed within two working days by an accuracy check on newly labelled cases, and each check either met the accuracy requirement or led to retraining.

In each weekly window since deployment, the loan-application model's production inputs showed no difference from its validation sample detectable by the agreed kernel two-sample test, at a significance level corrected for weekly repetition, and the same test detected the input shifts that had reduced the model's accuracy in pre-deployment trials.
Replayed on reference data alone, the drift monitor's kernel two-sample test raised false alarms at no more than the configured rate of one per quarter.

techniques.name: Rolling-Origin Evaluation
techniques.description: Rolling-origin evaluation, also called time-series cross-validation or backtesting, estimates how accurately a forecasting model will predict the future by repeatedly recreating the position it will be in when used: trained only on data up to a point in time, it forecasts the period that follows. The evaluator chooses a first forecast origin (the last time point the model may see) late enough to leave adequate training data, fits the model on the data up to that origin, forecasts every step of a fixed horizon ahead, for example one to seven days, and records the error at each lead time against the values later observed. The origin then moves forward by one step or a block of steps and the process repeats, with the model either refitted at each origin on all the data so far or on a window of fixed length (recalibration, in Tashman's terms), or kept unchanged and simply given the new observations as inputs (updating), whichever matches how it will be maintained in service. Because every forecast uses only data from before its origin, the method avoids the leakage of future information that randomly shuffled cross-validation can cause on time-ordered data, and because it uses many test periods rather than the single one of a fixed train-test split, its result depends less on which period happened to be held out. The output is the forecast error, under whatever error measure suits the forecast, broken down by lead time and by origin date for each candidate model, which supports claims about expected accuracy on unseen future data over a stated horizon and shows how that accuracy varies across seasons and conditions.

example_use_cases.description: A regional electricity distributor deciding whether to replace its regression model for day-ahead substation demand with a gradient-boosted model evaluates both over the last two years, with an origin each day at the time forecasts are issued, a horizon of the next 48 half-hours and weekly refitting, as planned for operation. It compares error at each lead time and in each season, and switches only after finding the new model better in winter peaks as well as on average.

A national weather service's post-processing team testing a machine-learning correction for station temperature forecasts places origins every day over three years, with lead times of one to ten days, and refits the correction monthly as it would in service. Error by lead time and by month shows whether the correction still helps at the longest lead times and whether its gain in winter holds in all three winters rather than one.

A hospital's operations analysts choosing a model to forecast emergency admissions one to fourteen days ahead for staff rotas compare a seasonal statistical model with a neural network, using weekly origins over two years that include two winter peaks. They report error at the seven-day lead time the rota planners use, and keep the simpler model because the neural network's advantage disappears at that horizon.

limitations.description: Refitting at every origin multiplies training cost by the number of origins: daily origins over two years means more than 700 fits. Machine-learning forecasters are often refitted only now and then and otherwise just fed new data, which Hewamalage et al. describe as common practice; that is cheaper but measures something different, so the refit schedule in the evaluation must match the one planned for deployment or the errors do not describe the deployed system.

The time-ordered split prevents leakage only through the split itself. Scaling, smoothing, decomposition, feature selection or tuning done on the whole series before splitting, or features summarising a period not yet over at the forecast time, still let future information in. Hewamalage et al. show a model beating the best possible forecast of a random walk only because a decomposition was fitted to the whole series; every such step must be redone within each origin.

Errors from neighbouring origins share most of their training data and, for multi-step horizons, overlapping test periods, so they are correlated: an average over hundreds of origins is less precise than the count suggests, and the spread across origins is not a confidence interval. Deciding whether one model beats another needs a test designed for serially correlated forecast errors, such as the Diebold-Mariano test, not a plain comparison of average errors.

The first origins have little training data, so their errors can overstate those of a model trained on the full history, and a short series leaves few test periods and a noisy average. For purely autoregressive models (past values as the only inputs) on stationary series, whose errors show no remaining autocorrelation, Bergmeir et al. show that standard k-fold cross-validation remains valid, and Hewamalage et al. recommend it for short series as it uses the data more efficiently.

It measures how the model would have performed over the history available, not how it will perform after a change that history does not contain, such as a new tariff, a replaced sensor or an abrupt structural break; Hewamalage et al. note that no evaluation design can anticipate a break that lies only in the future. Results should be stated for the periods and conditions they cover and repeated as new data arrive.
